summary: Working in Buddhist studies, Sinology, and Japanology, John Jorgensen was a researcher at Australian National University, taught Japanese studies at Griffith University, and served as Senior Research Associate at La Trobe University's China Studies Research Centre (attested 2019).

Specializing in Buddhist studies and Sinology, John Kieschnick held a post at the University of Bristol (~2005–2011) and became the Robert H. N. Ho Family Foundation Professor of Buddhist Studies at Stanford University around 2011.

Philosopher John Lane Bell earned his DPhil from the University of Oxford (1977–1980). He held posts at the London School of Economics (~1968–1989), the University of Western Ontario (~1989), and the University of Cambridge as Professor (2001).

Linguist and Indologist John Leyden studied at Edinburgh (~1790–1797) and St Andrews (MD ~1802), studying under Henry Thomas Colebrooke (~1806–1811). He became Professor of Hindustani at Fort William College (1806) and secretary at The Asiatic Society (~1810–1811).

Working in Indology and history/archaeology, John Lockwood Kipling taught at the Sir Jamsetjee Jeejebhoy School of Art (1865). From 1875 to 1893, he served as Principal of the National College of Arts and Curator of the Lahore Museum.

Active in philosophy, Indology, and religious studies, John M. Koller studied at the East-West Center under Shri Krishna Saksena, Charles Alexander Moore, and George T. Artola. He served as professor of philosophy at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute (attested 1988, 1999).

Specializing in history, archaeology, Japanology, and Buddhist studies, John M. Rosenfield earned his PhD at Harvard (1954–1959) under Benjamin Rowland. He was a professor at Harvard University and Curator of Oriental Art at Harvard Art Museums (1965–1991).

Specialist in Indology, history, and archaeology John Marshall studied at Cambridge and the British School at Athens under Arthur Evans. He served as Director General of the Archaeological Survey of India (1902–1931) and Fellow of King's College, Cambridge (~1927–1958).

Indologist and philosopher John McKenzie studied at the University of Aberdeen, New College, Edinburgh, and the University of Tübingen. He was Professor (1908) and Principal (1921–1944) at Wilson College, Mumbai, and Vice-Chancellor of the University of Mumbai (1931–1933).
Working in linguistics and Indology, John McKerrell served as Translator of Telugu and Kannaḍa for the Madras Civil Service in 1804 and was an ex officio member of the College of Fort St. George.

Active in religious studies and Indology, John Morrison earned a D.D. from the University of Calcutta. He served as Principal of Scottish Church College (1889–1904) and held lectureships at the University of Glasgow (1904) and University of Edinburgh.

John Muir studied at the East India Company College, Fort William College, and the universities of Glasgow and Bonn. He served in the Bengal Civil Service (1828–1853), led Sampurnanand Sanskrit University (1844), and was affiliated with Edinburgh (~1862–1882).

Working in religious studies and Indology, John Murdoch received an LL.D. from the University of Glasgow (1878). He served as Agent and Travelling Secretary in India for the Christian Vernacular Education Society (1858–1903) and was a Fellow of Madras University.

Indologist and religious studies scholar John Murray Mitchell studied at Marischal College and the University of Edinburgh. He taught at Wilson College, Mumbai (1844–1866) and served as Principal of Duff College (1868–1873).
Working in Tibetology and Buddhist studies, John Myrdhin Reynolds completed traditional studies under Yongdzin Tenzin Namdak, Dudjom Rinpoche, and Namkhai Norbu.

Active in religious studies and Indology, John N. Carpenter was a missionary for the Church Mission Society. He served as Principal of St. Paul's Divinity School (1900) and Emmanuel College (1916–1922), and held a post at St. John's College, Agra.

Specialist in Indology, philosophy, and religious studies John Nemec earned degrees from Rochester, UC Santa Barbara, Oxford, and Pennsylvania (PhD 2005), studying under Alexis Sanderson and Ludo Rocher. In 2004, he joined the University of Virginia faculty.

Linguist John Okell studied at The Queen's College, Oxford, and under Hla Pe, Anna J. Allott, and Richard Keith Sprigg. He served as a research associate at SOAS University of London from 1959 to 1999.

Scholar of Buddhist and religious studies John P. Keenan earned his PhD at the University of Wisconsin–Madison under Minoru Kiyota. He was a Research Fellow at Nanzan University (1983–1986) and later taught as a professor at Middlebury College.

Indologist and linguist John Peile studied at Christ's College, Cambridge, and under Theodor Benfey at Göttingen. At Cambridge, he became Reader of Comparative Philology (1884–1893), Master of Christ's College (1887), and President of Newnham College (~1890–1909).
